title: Celsus passes over the prophecies
source_text: Μετὰ ταῦτ᾿ οὐκ οἶδ᾿ ὅπως τὸ μέγιστον περὶ τῆς συστάσεως τοῦ Ἰησοῦ κεφάλαιον, ὡς ὅτι ἐπροφητεύθη ὑπὸ τῶν παρὰ Ἰουδαίοις προφητῶν, Μωϋσέως καὶ τῶν μετ᾿ αὐτὸν ἢ καὶ πρὸ Μω(??)σέως, παραπίπτει ἑκὼν, ὡς οἶμαι τῷ μὴ δύνασθαι ἀπαντᾶν πρὸς λόγον ὡς οὐδὲ Ἰουδαῖοι οὐδ᾿ ὅσαι αἱρέσεις οὐ βούλονται πεπροφητεῦσθαι τὸν Ἰησοῦν. τάχα δὲ οὐδὲ ᾔδει τὰς περὶ τοῦ Ἰησοῦ προφητείας· οὐκ ἂν γὰρ καταβαλὼν τὰ ὑπὸ Χριστιανῶν λεγόμενα, ὅτι πολλοὶ προφῆται προεῖπον περὶ τῆς τοῦ σωτῆρος ἐπιδημίας, περιέθηκε τῷ τοῦ Ἰουδαίου προσώπῳ ἃ ἥρμοζε Σαμαρεῖ μᾶλλον εἰπεῖν ἢ Σαδδουκαίῳ· καὶ οὐκ ἂν Ἰουδαῖος ὁ ἐν τῇ προσωποποΐᾳ ἔφασκεν· ἀλλ᾿ εἶπεν ἐμὸς προφήτης ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις ποτὲ ὅτι ἥξει θεοῦ υἱὸς, τῶν ὁσίων κριτὴς καὶ τῶν ἀδίκων κολαστής. οὐ γὰρ εἷς προφήτης τὰ περὶ Χριστοῦ ἐπροφήτευσε· κἂν οἱ μόνου δὲ Μωϋσέως παραδεχόμενοι τὰς βίβλους Σαμαρεῖς ἢ Σαδδουκαῖοι φάσκωσιν ἐν ἐκείναις πεπροφητεῦσθαι τὸν Χριστὸν, ἀλλ᾿ οὔτι γε ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις, τοῖς μηδέπω ὀνομασθεῖσι κατὰ τὸν Μωϋσέως χρόνον, ἡ προφητεία λέλεκτο. εἴη τοίνυν πάντας τοὺς τοῦ λόγου κατηγόρους ἐν τοσαύτῃ εἶναι ἀγνοίᾳ οὐ μόνον τῶν πραγμάτων ἀλλὰ καὶ ψιλῶν τῶν γραμμάτων τῆς γραφῆς καὶ κατηγορεῖν χριστιανισμοῦ, ἵνα μηδὲ τὴν τυχοῦσαν πιθανότητα ὁ λόγος αὐτῶν ἔχῃ, δυναμένην τοὺς ἀνερματίστους καὶ „πρὸς καιρὸν“ πιστεύοντας ἀφιστάνειν οὐ τῆς πίστεως ἀλλὰ τῆς ὀλιγοπιστίας. Ἰουδαῖος δὲ οὐκ ἂν ὁμολογήσαι ὅτι προφήτης τις εἶπεν ἥξειν θεοῦ υἱόν· ὃ γὰρ λέγουσιν, ἐστὶν ὅτι ἥξει ὁ Χριστὸς τοῦ θεοῦ. καὶ πολλάκις γε ζητοῦσι πρὸς ἡμᾶς εὐθέως περὶ υἱοῦ θεοῦ, ὡς οὐδενὸς ὄντος τοιούτου οὐδὲ προφητευθέντος. καὶ οὐ τοῦτό φαμεν, ὅτι οὐ προφητεύεται υἱὸς θεοῦ, ἀλλ᾿ ὅτι οὐχ ἁρμοζόντως τῷ Ἰουδαϊκῷ προσώπῳ, μὴ ὁμολογοῦντι τὸ τοιοῦτο, περιέθηκε τὸ εἶπεν ἐμὸς προφήτης ἐν Ἱεροσολύμοις ποτὲ ὅτι ἥξει θεοῦ υἱός
pass_a_gloss: After these things, I know not how, the greatest heading (κεφάλαιον) concerning the commendation/proof (σύστασις) of Jesus, namely that he was prophesied (ἐπροφητεύθη) by the prophets among the Jews, Moses and those after him or even before Moses, he passes by (παραπίπτει) willingly (ἑκών), as I think, through not being able to meet (ἀπαντᾶν) the argument (λόγον), as neither Jews nor all the sects (αἱρέσεις) who do not wish Jesus to have been prophesied [can]. Perhaps he did not even know the prophecies about Jesus; for he would not, having laid down/taken up (καταβαλών) the things said by Christians, that many prophets foretold the Saviour's coming (ἐπιδημία), have put on (περιέθηκε) the person (πρόσωπον) of the Jew what would rather fit a Samaritan to say or a Sadducee; and the Jew in the impersonation (προσωποποιΐα) would not have said: 'But my prophet once said in Jerusalem that a son of God will come (ἥξει), judge (κριτής) of the holy (ὁσίων) and punisher (κολαστής) of the unjust.' For not one prophet prophesied the things about Christ; and even if the Samaritans or Sadducees, accepting only the books of Moses, say the Christ was prophesied in those, yet not at least in Jerusalem, not yet named in Moses' time, had the prophecy been spoken. May it be (εἴη) then that all the accusers of the word/teaching (λόγου) are in such ignorance not only of the matters but also of the bare letters (ψιλῶν τῶν γραμμάτων) of Scripture, and accuse Christianity, so that their argument may have not even chance plausibility (πιθανότης) able to draw away (ἀφιστάνειν) the unballasted (ἀνερματίστους) and those believing 'for a season' (πρὸς καιρόν), not from faith (πίστεως) but from little faith (ὀλιγοπιστίας). A Jew would not confess that some prophet said a son of God would come; what they say is that the Christ of God will come. And often they inquire/dispute (ζητοῦσι) with us straightway about a son of God, as none such existing nor prophesied. And we do not say this, that a son of God is not prophesied, but that not fittingly (οὐχ ἁρμοζόντως) to the Jewish person, not confessing such a thing, did he attach 'my prophet once said in Jerusalem that a son of God will come.'
pass_b_english: After this, I do not know how, he willingly passes over the most important point in the case for Jesus: that he was foretold by the prophets of the Jews, by Moses and those after him, and even by those before Moses. I think he does so because he cannot answer the argument, any more than the Jews can, or the sects that do not want Jesus to have been foretold. Perhaps he did not even know the prophecies about Jesus. For had he taken up what Christians say, that many prophets foretold the Saviour's coming, he would not have put into the mouth of his Jew words that would have suited a Samaritan or a Sadducee better. Nor would the Jew of his invented speech have said: "But a prophet of mine once said in Jerusalem that a Son of God will come, judge of the holy and punisher of the unrighteous."

For it was not just one prophet who foretold the things about Christ. And even if the Samaritans or the Sadducees, who accept only the books of Moses, were to say that the Christ was foretold in those books, still the prophecy was certainly not spoken in Jerusalem, which had not yet been named in the time of Moses.

If only, then, all who accuse our teaching were as ignorant as this, not only of the facts but even of the bare letter of Scripture, and accused Christianity in that state, so that their argument might lack even ordinary persuasiveness, the kind able to draw away the unsteady and those who believe "for a while" (Luke 8:13), not from faith but from little faith.

But a Jew would not admit that any prophet said that a Son of God would come. What they say is that the Christ of God will come. And indeed they often argue with us straight away about the Son of God, as though there were no such being and none had been foretold. We are not saying that a Son of God is not foretold, but that Celsus has given the Jewish character, who does not admit any such thing, words that do not fit him: "A prophet of mine once said in Jerusalem that a Son of God will come."

choices.choice: The staged text has Μω(??)σέως, read Μωσέως (Moses). καταβαλών ('having laid down / taken up') is awkward; the sense required is that Celsus, had he engaged with the Christian claim, would not have written as he did; rendered 'had he taken up'. Some editors prefer καταλαβών ('grasped'); either gives the same sense. The clause ὡς οὐδὲ Ἰουδαῖοι οὐδ᾿ ὅσαι αἱρέσεις οὐ βούλονται πεπροφητεῦσθαι τὸν Ἰησοῦν is elliptical: 'just as neither the Jews nor the sects that do not want Jesus foretold [can answer it]'. The sects meant are probably those that rejected the Old Testament (e.g. the Marcionites); not named in the Greek. 'Our teaching' renders τοῦ λόγου. The phrase πρὸς καιρὸν πιστεύοντας is from Luke 8:13 (οἳ πρὸς καιρὸν πιστεύουσιν); cf. Mark 4:17 (πρόσκαιροι). ἀνερματίστους, literally 'unballasted', is rendered 'unsteady'. Celsus's words are given as his Jew's direct speech (εἶπεν ἐμὸς προφήτης...); 'a prophet of mine' renders ἐμὸς προφήτης. 'Son of God' is capitalised throughout as the house style requires, though Origen's point is that a Jew would not use the phrase.
οὐ τοῦτό φαμεν, ὅτι ... ἀλλ᾿ ὅτι: 'We do not say this because ... but because' (causal misreading) corrected to 'We are not saying that ... but that'
ζητοῦσι πρὸς ἡμᾶς: 'question us at once' changed to 'argue with us straight away'
οὐ γὰρ εἷς προφήτης: 'not one prophet' changed to 'not just one prophet' to avoid a 'no prophet' misreading
εἴη: archaic 'Would that' changed to 'If only'
Luke 8:13 (πρὸς καιρὸν πιστεύουσιν) checked; Celsus's Jew's words quoted and attributed as the Greek frames them
